clue.text: Girl tangled with men eaus ing trouble in plane

definitions.note: describes the creature itself: the one causing trouble in an aircraft

indicators.note: tangled says the letters of the two words are knotted together into a new order

explanation.surface: A girl getting mixed up with men who are making a nuisance of themselves on a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangled' shuffles GIRL and MEN together. The definition is a description of the imp that RAF airmen blamed for mechanical faults.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmen's folklore blamed unexplained mechanical faults in aircraft on a mischievous imp, so the word names a saboteur of planes.

clue.text: Earth goddess 'needs hair-dye? Hell:

parts.note: Ge, or Gaia, is the Greek goddess of the earth
henna is a reddish dye used on hair

explanation.surface: Even the earth goddess needs her hair coloured? Damnation!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hell' reads as an exclamation; it is the definition, the biblical place of torment.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible this valley outside Jerusalem became a name for the place of eternal punishment.

clue.text: A philosophical type, Pater's Marius

definitions.meaning: a follower of Epicurus, whose philosophy sought pleasure in moderation
Walter Pater's 1885 novel is called 'Marius the' followed by this word

explanation.walkthrough: Walter Pater was a Victorian critic whose novel 'Marius the Epicurean' is set in ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple of Epicurus is one sense; the other is the title character's epithet in Walter Pater's novel.

clue.text: Old refugee takes to bingo

parts.note: Lot fled the destruction of Sodom in the Old Testament
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly refugee takes up a game of bingo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old refugee' is a biblical figure: Lot, who escaped Sodom while his wife turned to salt.
explanation.definitionFit: This game of drawing numbers and marking them off on cards is another name for bingo.

clue.text: A hundred actors in trouble with drugs.

indicators.note: trouble, as a verb, means stir up, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A hundred actors who get into difficulty over drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' looks like one phrase, but 'in' joins the anagram fodder with C and ACTORS, and 'trouble' alone stirs them.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcotics are drugs that dull the senses, often illegal ones such as opiates.

clue.text: Epic hero advocating lycanthropy, we hear ?

indicators.note: we hear tells the solver to go by how the phrase sounds when spoken

parts.note: lycanthropy is turning into a wolf, so advocating it is urging someone to 'be a wolf'

explanation.surface: A legendary hero who recommends turning into a werewolf, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be a wolf', said quickly, sounds like the name of the warrior of the Old English epic.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the warrior who kills Grendel in the Old English poem named after him.

clue.text: Are night fliers so crazy?

parts.note: asks whether creatures flying at night have the quality of their name, a word meaning mad

explanation.surface: A question about whether pilots on night flights are mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'night fliers' suggests pilots; they are the nocturnal mammals, and an adjective built from them means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means eccentric or mad, as if one had bats in the belfry.

clue.text: Nell Gwyn's male Irish 'counterpart ?

parts.note: Nell Gwyn sold oranges in a theatre; a man doing the same would share his title with an Ulster Protestant loyalist

explanation.surface: An Irishman who matches the famous actress and royal mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Gwyn, Charles II's mistress, began as an orange-seller at Drury Lane, so a male version is an orange man; joined up it names a member of the Orange Order in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Protestant Orange Order of Ireland, named after William of Orange, is described.

clue.text: Marriage with Jack, the ensign

definitions.meaning: a joining of two people as spouses
followed by 'Jack' it names the British national flag

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is completed by the clue's word 'Jack': the Union Jack is the British flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding is a joining together, and the British flag is called the Union Jack.

clue.text: Olivia's fool consumes four, enjoying the banquet

indicators.note: consumes means the fool's name swallows the next piece inside it

parts.note: Feste is the clown in Olivia's household in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Olivia's jester tucks into four courses at the feast.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste is the jester in Twelfth Night; 'consumes' fits the banquet picture while putting IV inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking part in a feast with good cheer is being in a festive or celebratory mood.

clue.text: Elevator blown up

definitions.meaning: a device or tackle for lifting loads
in Hamlet's phrase '... with his own petard', an engineer is blown up by his own bomb

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition relies on Shakespeare's 'hoist with his own petard', where the word means lifted into the air by an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifting tackle is one sense; the other is the old past participle from Hamlet's line about being blown sky-high by one's own petard.

clue.text: Old Roman had to get one in the net to win

definitions.text: Old Roman had to get one in the net to win

parts.words: Old Roman had to get one in the net to win
parts.note: an arena fighter of ancient Rome armed with a net and trident, who won by entangling his opponent

explanation.surface: A Roman footballer needing a goal to take the match.
explanation.walkthrough: The football picture of scoring a goal misleads; the 'net' is a real weapon, the fighter's name coming from Latin rete, net.
explanation.definitionFit: This class of gladiator fought with a weighted net and trident, trapping his opponent to win the bout.

clue.text: In coining words you are soundly creating medical science

indicators.note: In places the following piece inside the word for coining words

parts.note: the coining of new words is neology

indicators.note: soundly says the phrase is replaced by letters that sound like it

parts.note: said aloud, 'you are' is the letters U and R, as in text-speak

explanation.surface: Someone inventing terms is told they are building up a branch of medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' turns 'you are' into the two letters UR, which go 'In' NEOLOGY, the coining of words.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the branch of medicine dealing with the nervous system and its disorders.

clue.text: Good or' evil, spirits in general before eleven

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the second in the answer

parts.note: II is eleven in the sense of the two strokes of the Roman numeral, read as I and I side by side

explanation.surface: Spirits, good or bad, generally appearing before eleven o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: Eleven is written as two numeral ones side by side, which look like the Roman two strokes; the comma after 'evil' ends the definition, so 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arabian tales the jinn, spirits who may help or harm people, are called by this plural.

clue.text: Proficient in making grade Ptolemaic Theory

indicators.note: in says the answer is found inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Being expert at reaching a high standard in Ptolemy's astronomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The run grADE PTolemaic holds the answer across the word break; 'making' and 'Theory' only dress the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Being highly skilled at something is being expert or proficient in it.

clue.text: Gloria Mundi's just passing

parts.note: recalls the Latin tag 'sic transit gloria mundi', thus passes the glory of the world

explanation.surface: Someone called Gloria Mundi is merely walking by.
explanation.walkthrough: Gloria Mundi looks like a woman's name; it is the Latin 'glory of the world', which the proverb says is fleeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fleeting or lasting only a short time is described, as worldly glory is in the proverb.

clue.text: Put out a piece of furniture in front

indicators.note: front puts the little word at the head of the furniture word

parts.note: taken as written
a commode is a chest of drawers or a chair concealing a chamber pot

explanation.surface: Moving a bit of furniture out to the front of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like an instruction to shift the furniture; it means to inconvenience someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To inconvenience or disturb someone is to put them out.

clue.text: This paper may be blank

parts.note: names both a thick drawing paper and a round of ammunition that can be fired without a bullet

explanation.surface: A sheet of paper that has nothing written on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blank' suggests an empty sheet; a blank is also a round with no bullet, and the word names that round as well as the drawing paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A firearm round is this, and a blank one has no bullet; there is also a stiff drawing paper of the same name.

clue.text: By no means Pliable he who never reached Slough

definitions.text: By no means Pliable he who never reached Slough

parts.words: By no means Pliable he who never reached Slough
parts.note: in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, Pliable sank in the Slough of Despond, while his stubborn companion turned home before it

explanation.surface: Someone inflexible who never made it to the town of Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London, but here it is Bunyan's Slough of Despond; the stubborn neighbour of Christian gave up before reaching it.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian's neighbour in Pilgrim's Progress is named for his stubbornness, the opposite of his companion Pliable.

clue.text: A candidate's solicitor

parts.note: not a lawyer but someone who solicits votes door to door on behalf of an election candidate

explanation.surface: The lawyer acting for a person standing for election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solicitor' suggests a British lawyer; here it means one who solicits, asking voters for support.
explanation.definitionFit: At election time a party worker goes round asking residents for their votes on behalf of the candidate.

clue.text: Examples of political

parts.note: with the next clue's 'joinery' it describes both a body of senior ministers and a piece of furniture made by a joiner

explanation.surface: Instances of political goings-on, continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 20 down: the word is a group of senior ministers and also a cupboard, the work of a cabinet-maker's joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior ministers of a government form one, and a cupboard with shelves and doors made by a joiner is another.

clue.text: This organ's pneumatically operated

parts.note: the organ is not a musical instrument but the nose, worked by breath, and the word describes things relating to it

explanation.surface: A church organ powered by air.
explanation.walkthrough: Organs are blown pneumatically, so the instrument springs to mind; the organ is the nose, through which air passes.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to the nose, through which air is breathed in and out.

clue.text: … and an old shoe-maker's joinery

parts.note: the joinery of a shoemaker is the thong that fastens a shoe, an archaic word

explanation.surface: A cobbler's woodworking, continuing the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoes are not made by joiners: the 'joinery' is the strap that joins the shoe on the foot, an old word familiar from the Bible's 'shoe's latchet'.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic term for a thong or lace that fastens a sandal or shoe is used in the Bible.

clue.text: Ruth's victims in a wood

parts.note: points both to the baseball player called the Babe and to the two children of the ballad who perish in a wood

explanation.surface: People who fell prey to a woman called Ruth in a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth suggests a woman; it is the American baseball star Babe Ruth. The children's tale 'The Babes in the Wood' supplies the victims.
explanation.definitionFit: Babe was baseball star Ruth's nickname, and the abandoned children of the old tale who die in a forest are its babes.

clue.text: Most apt of those famous last words in Middlemarch ?

definitions.text: Most apt of those famous last words in Middlemarch

parts.words: Most apt of those famous last words in Middlemarch
parts.note: Caesar's dying 'Et tu' phrase was spoken on the Ides, the middle of March, and its final word is the one that fits

explanation.surface: Picking the best-known closing lines of George Eliot's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlemarch is George Eliot's novel, but here it means the middle of March: Caesar, killed on the Ides, said 'Et tu, Brute?', whose last word fits.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the vocative of Brutus, the last word of Caesar's reproach to his friend among the assassins.

clue.text: This bomb-slinger losing his head might make mistakes

definitions.text: This bomb-slinger losing his head might make mistakes

parts.words: This bomb-slinger losing his head might make mistakes
parts.note: a bomber's title without its first letter reads as a made-up word for someone who makes errors

explanation.surface: A bomber who panics is liable to slip up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing his head' means panicking in the surface, but it drops the first letter, leaving ERRORIST, one who errs.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who uses bombs and violence to spread fear for political ends is described.

clue.text: What any (land)lord has

parts.note: a peer has a rank such as earl, and a landowner has legal ownership deeds, both called by one word

explanation.surface: A question about what every landlord owns.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket lets the clue read as lord or landlord: a lord bears a rank, a landlord holds the deeds proving ownership.
explanation.definitionFit: A noble rank such as baron is one, and the legal right of ownership of land is another.

clue.text: Tender of metal for French railways

parts.note: taken as written
French railways are 'chemins de fer', roads of iron, and fer is French for iron

explanation.surface: A bid for a contract to supply metal for the French railway network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like a business bid; it is the definition. 'Metal for French' alone gives FER; the railways hint at chemin de fer.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender something is to proffer it, and a tender is a proposal or bid.

clue.text: In Scotland no use a boy getting seasick

parts.note: na is the Scots word for no
taken as written
Ted is a boy's name

explanation.surface: In Scotland there is no point in a lad going to sea if he gets queasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being seasick means feeling sick to the stomach on a moving ship.

clue.text: This back is in retrospect showy and quick

definitions.meaning: put this word before 'back' and you get a scene looking back in time

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a word puzzle: add 'back' to the answer to get a cinematic look into the past.
explanation.definitionFit: A film's flashback looks to the past; the word alone means gaudy or ostentatious, and as in 'in a flash', speedy.

clue.text: Board's supporter sorts letters

indicators.note: sorts means arranges the letters into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A post-room worker supporting the board sorts the mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board's supporter' suggests a company backer; it is a stand holding up a table top.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame of legs and a crossbar is used to hold up a tabletop or plank.

clue.text: Art working for money? That's serious!

definitions.meaning: in old English 'thou art earning' can be put as thou ..., so art working for money is that verb form

explanation.walkthrough: 'Art' looks like painting; it is the archaic verb as in 'thou art'.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic 'thou earnest' is the second-person form of earning wages; the adjective means sincere and grave.
